standard.title: Character, setting and plot tension
standard.description: discuss how authors develop characters, setting and plot tension in literary texts, and the connection between setting and mood
standard.prior_knowledge: Students discuss how authors use language and illustrations to portray characters and how settings influence mood (AC9E3LE03). They have not yet examined how character, setting and plot tension work together as interconnected authorial choices.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can discuss how authors develop characters through action, dialogue and description; how setting choices create mood; and how plot tension is built through conflict, pacing and structure — explaining the connections between these elements.

nodes.label: Character development techniques
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify at least three techniques authors use to develop characters and explain how each reveals character.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two techniques an author uses to develop a character (e.g. what the character says and what they do) and explain what each reveals.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss the full range of character development techniques — dialogue, action, direct description, narrator commentary, other characters' reactions — across at least two characters in a text, explaining how each technique reveals different dimensions of character.
wider: Compare how character is developed differently in a picture book (through illustration and sparse text) versus a chapter book (through extended description and dialogue)
Examine how First Nations Australian authors develop characters through relationship with Country and community, and how this differs from individualised Western character development

response_modes.reason: Character development awareness is built through encountering many examples across many texts. Students who have only seen one or two techniques for character development apply them too broadly in their own writing.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of character development techniques — and how different authors use them differently — is rich territory. First Nations Australian character-Country relationships are a significantly different and valuable dimension.
success_criteria: Can name at least three character development techniques and give an example of each from a text
Can explain what a specific technique reveals about a character that another technique would not

nodes.label: Setting and mood
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how an author's setting choices create mood, identifying specific language and visual features that produce the mood.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the mood created by a setting in a literary text and name one specific language or visual feature that creates it.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how setting choices — time of day, weather, landscape, sensory details, colour — create mood across a range of literary texts, explaining how the author's specific choices produce specific emotional atmospheres.
wider: Compare how two authors create contrasting moods through setting description in texts in the same genre (e.g. two adventure stories with different settings)
Examine how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors portray Country as an active participant in setting mood, and discuss how this differs from Western landscape description
success_criteria: Can name the mood created by a setting and identify at least one specific language feature (e.g. a specific adjective or sensory detail) that creates it
Does not just name the setting — connects specific features to the mood produced

nodes.label: Plot tension
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how an author builds plot tension through conflict, pacing and structural choices, and explain the connection between tension and reader engagement.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the main conflict in a text and explain one way the author builds tension around it.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how authors build plot tension across a text through conflict (character vs character, character vs self, character vs situation), pacing choices (short sentences, cliffhangers, delayed resolution) and structural choices (chapter endings, withholding information).
wider: Compare how tension is built differently in two texts in the same genre — what techniques are shared and what differs?
Map the tension curve of a text, identifying moments of rising tension, release and climax, and analyse the structural choices the author made to create this shape

response_modes.reason: Understanding tension as a constructed, technical product of specific authorial choices requires a reasoning scaffold. Students instinctively feel tension but need explicit analysis of what creates it.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Plot tension analysis — including tension mapping and technique comparison across texts — is genuinely rich territory that connects character, setting and structure.
success_criteria: Can identify the main conflict in a text and name one technique the author uses to build tension
Does not describe tension as just 'exciting' — can explain what the author did to create the feeling
